sections.b: Malachi is the last of the Twelve Prophets, four chapters in English (three in Hebrew) and 55 verses. In six disputes with the priests and people of Persian-period Judah, the LORD charges them, they reply "But you say...", and he answers. The topics are his love for Jacob against Edom (1:2-5), bad offerings and the covenant with Levi (1:6-2:9), betrayal in marriage (2:10-16), the God of justice and the coming messenger (2:17-3:5), the tithe (3:6-12), and the sun of righteousness (3:13-4:3). It ends with Moses and Elijah (4:4-6). The name Malachi means 'my messenger' (3:1) and is perhaps the book's title rather than the prophet's name.

common: The book comes from the Persian period, after the Temple was finished in about 515 BC.
uncommon: Malachi was Ezra the scribe, as the Targum Jonathan says (Jerome also discusses it), or Mordecai, as one Talmud view has it.

sections.b: Malachi uses the word mal'akh, 'messenger', in four ways: as the book's title (1:1), of the priest as the LORD's messenger (2:7), of the figure who clears the road before the LORD (3:1), and of the 'messenger of the covenant' who comes with the Lord to his temple (3:1). Scholars debate whether these are one, two or three figures. The Gospels read the first as John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10) and many Christians read the second as Christ; Jewish tradition reads the forerunner as Elijah (4:5).

Exodus 23:20 has the LORD send an angel (mal'akh) ahead of Israel to keep it on the way, and the Gospels blend that verse with Malachi 3:1 in their quotation (Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27). The messenger of the covenant may therefore be the angel who carries out the covenant's judgments. Isaiah 40:3 clears 'the way of the LORD' in the wilderness, and Mark joins it to Malachi.

common: The messenger who clears the road is a forerunner distinct from the LORD.
uncommon: All the 'messengers' are one figure: the priest of the future, who purifies Levi.

sections.b: Malachi 4:2 promises those who fear the LORD's name that 'a sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings'. Jews read it of the LORD's justice as a light that burns the wicked and heals the righteous (Avodah Zarah 3b-4a); Christians have read it of Christ since the fathers, and Zechariah's song about the 'Dawn from on high' (Luke 1:78) is often paired with it. The winged sun disc was a common symbol in Egypt, Assyria and Persia, which may lie behind the image.

common: The image is of the LORD's saving justice coming like the dawn.
uncommon: The image deliberately takes over the winged sun symbol of the empire and gives it to the LORD.

sections.b: Malachi begins with Edom. The LORD's love for Jacob is shown by Edom's ruin: its mountains are a waste, and whatever Edom builds the LORD will tear down; it will be called 'the Territory of Wickedness'. The Hebrew 'hated' means 'not chosen', as with Leah (Genesis 29:30-33). Paul quotes the line in Romans 9:13. The passage is about nations; it does not say what became of any individual Edomite.

'Jacob' in Malachi is both the patriarch loved against Esau (1:2) and the nation: 'the tents of Jacob' (2:12) and 'the sons of Jacob' who have not come to an end (3:6). A possible word play links the people's robbing God (qava') to Jacob's name, as the verb of Jacob's supplanting uses the same consonants in a different order (3:8; Genesis 27:36). That link is Claude's theory in the notes.

The Hebrew line 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' speaks of two peoples and of land, in the language of covenant. Paul quotes it in Romans 9:13 to speak of God's free choice. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and Methodist writers read the relation of that choice to human response differently; the card on Malachi 1:2-3 sets them side by side. Hebrew 'hate' can mean the opposite of 'choose', as in Deuteronomy 21:15-17.

Malachi 1:6-2:9 is the book's longest speech and it is to the priests. They accept blind, lame and stolen animals (Leviticus 22:17-25), treat the altar's food as despicable, and teach with partiality. The LORD holds up the covenant with Levi as a model: life and peace, true teaching, a mouth that guards knowledge, a man who turned many from guilt (2:5-7). The priest is called the messenger of the LORD of Armies. The book uses 'priest' and 'Levi' for the same body, like Deuteronomy, and the debate whether this reflects a quarrel between priests and Levites is open.

sections.b: No law text gives 'a covenant with Levi' by that name. The nearest are Levi's blessing (Deuteronomy 33:8-11), the Levites' zeal after the golden calf (Exodus 32:26-29), Phinehas's covenant of peace (Numbers 25:12-13) and Jeremiah's promise to the Levitical priests (Jeremiah 33:17-22). Malachi 2:4-8 says the priests have ruined it, and 3:3 says the LORD will purify the descendants of Levi.

uncommon: Malachi takes the side of the Levites against the priestly family of Aaron.

sections.h: Bad offerings and a pure offering
sections.b: The law required an unblemished animal (Leviticus 22:17-25). Malachi shows priests accepting blind, lame, sick and stolen ones and asks if they would give the same to their governor (1:8). He says he would rather the doors were shut than have such fires on his altar (1:10), and sets against it 'a pure offering' brought to his name among the nations (1:11). The Hebrew word for 'offering' in 1:10, 1:11, 1:13, 2:12, 2:13, 3:3 and 3:4 is minchah, which is 'grain offering' in Leviticus 2; the note at 1:10 explains why Malachi's Plain says 'offering'.

The Didache (14:1-3) quotes Malachi 1:11 and 1:14 for the Lord's Day thanksgiving, and Justin Martyr and Irenaeus read the 'pure offering' of the Eucharist. The Council of Trent (Session 22) and the Catechism (1350) cite it for the Mass. Lutheran, Reformed and Baptist writers read it of the worship of the church in prayer and praise, not of a repeated sacrifice. The card on Malachi 1:11 sets the views side by side.

Malachi 1:11 says that in every place incense is being brought to the LORD's name. The Hebrew can mean the worship of Jews outside Jerusalem (the Jewish temple at Elephantine in Egypt offered incense in the 5th century BC), the nations' worship, or a future time; Christian writers took it of the church's prayer (compare Revelation 8:3-4).

Malachi mentions four covenants: the covenant with Levi (2:4-8), the covenant of 'our ancestors' that men profane by betrayal (2:10), the marriage covenant ('the wife of your covenant', 2:14), and the 'messenger of the covenant' (3:1). The first is the priests': 'life and peace' (2:5) echoes the covenant of peace with Phinehas (Numbers 25:12-13). The second is Israel's, the third a husband's. The Plain keeps the one English 'covenant'.

Malachi is built on a charge, an objection and a reply. Eight times the people answer 'But you say' (1:2, 6, 7; 2:14, 17; 3:7, 8, 13). Adrian Graffy's book on the disputation speech in the prophets (1984) reserves that name for the prophets' quoting of the people's words in order to refute them; in Malachi the people's own words are quoted and answered, one by one.

sections.b: The passage speaks of betrayal (bagad) of a brother, of the LORD's holy place by marrying the daughter of a foreign god, and of 'the wife of your youth', whom the LORD has stood as witness for. It calls marriage a covenant (2:14). The hardest part is 2:16: 'he hates sending away' (the Plain), or 'if you hate her, send her away' (the Greek, the Vulgate, the first words of a scroll, and Rashi and the Targum Jonathan). The Talmud (Gittin 90) records both readings. Jesus's teaching on divorce in Matthew 19:3-9 and Mark 10:2-12 is often read with it. The card on Malachi 2:14-16 shows the churches' views.

common: The passage forbids the casual divorce of a Judean wife.
uncommon: The passage permits divorce for a hated wife, with a warning of violence.

sections.b: Malachi 2:11 says Judah has profaned what is holy to the LORD and 'married the daughter of a foreign god'. It can mean intermarriage with women of other peoples (Ezra 9-10; Nehemiah 13:23-27) or the figure of Judah's idolatry. Malachi 3:5 meanwhile condemns those who push aside the resident foreigner, so the book treats foreigners as both a danger to worship and a group with a claim to justice.

The LORD says the nation is robbing him in the tithe and the contribution, and asks for the whole tithe in the storehouse so that there is food in his house. He invites a test: he will open the windows of the heavens and rebuke the devourer. The setting is the Levites and priests short of food in the Persian period (Nehemiah 13:10-13). The popular use of the verse as a promise of personal wealth for giving (the prosperity gospel) does not follow the Hebrew, which speaks to a nation and promises harvest. The card on Malachi 3:8-10 sets out the churches' views.

uncommon: The Hebrew verb 'rob' (qava') may play on Jacob's name, as Claude's note suggests.

sections.b: The priests are warned that the LORD will curse their blessings (2:2) and the nation is 'cursed with the curse' (3:9), the language of the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28. The reversal, if the tithe is brought, is open windows of heaven and no devourer (3:10-11), the blessings of Deuteronomy 28:1-14.

The LORD promises to rebuke 'the devourer' so that the crops and the vine will not fail (3:11). The Hebrew is a plain participle, 'the eater': a crop pest such as the locust, one of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:38-42), like the locusts of Joel and Amos 4:9. Haggai describes drought and blight in the same period (Haggai 1:10-11; 2:16-17).

sections.h: A people who fear the LORD
sections.b: In 3:16-18 a group within the community speaks together while others say serving God is pointless. The LORD records them in a scroll of remembrance and calls them his 'private treasure' (segullah), the title used for all Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5). The line between the righteous and the wicked, once seen, again becomes visible (3:18).

Malachi 3:16 says a 'scroll of remembrance' was written for those who fear the LORD. Persian courts kept records of those who served the king (Esther 6:1-3), and the Bible speaks of heavenly books in several places (Exodus 32:32-33; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 7:10; 12:1; Revelation 20:12).

The book ends with the LORD's promise to send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day, to turn the hearts of fathers and sons to each other. Sirach 48:10 and the Mishnah (Eduyot 8:7) refer to it. The Gospels apply it to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10-13; Mark 9:11-13; Luke 1:17); John himself denies he is Elijah (John 1:21). The card on Malachi 4:5-6 sets out the traditions.

The Gospels quote Malachi 3:1 of John: 'Look, I am sending my messenger before your face' (Matthew 11:10; Luke 7:27), blended with Exodus 23:20, and Mark begins with the same blend (Mark 1:2). Matthew has Jesus call John the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14), and Luke has the angel say John will go ahead of the Lord 'with Elijah's spirit and power' (Luke 1:17).
sections.refs: Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5-6; Matthew 11:10-14; Mark 1:2; Luke 1:17; Luke 7:27

sections.b: Malachi pictures the day in two ways: as fire for the proud and evildoers, who will be stubble with neither root nor branch (4:1), and as a rising sun that heals those who fear the name (4:2). The phrase 'great and awesome day' (4:5) is Joel's (Joel 2:31). The refiner's fire (3:2-3) belongs to the same day: it purifies Levi first.

The book's last command is to remember the law of Moses at Horeb, with its 'rules and rulings', for all Israel (4:4). 'Horeb' is Deuteronomy's name for the mountain. Many read 4:4-6 as an editor's close to the Twelve or the Prophets, which joins them to the law.

sections.h: Malachi and the Second Temple's daily life
sections.b: Haggai and Zechariah were about building the Temple; Malachi is about running it. The altar's food, the priests' teaching, the tithe, the storehouse and the Levites' shares are the daily concerns of the finished Temple. Nehemiah 13:4-13 describes the same abuses in the 5th century BC.

Malachi 1:8 mentions 'your governor' (pechah), the Persian-appointed official of the province of Judah, and tells the priests to offer him their bad animals. The LORD calls himself 'a great king' (1:14), which some read as an echo of the Persian ruler's title (an inference; the psalms use the phrase too). The book fits the province of Yehud under Persian rule.

sections.h: Where is the God of justice?
sections.b: The people ask 'Where is the God of justice?' (2:17). The LORD answers that he is coming to judge sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, those who cheat workers, and those who wrong the widow, the fatherless and the resident foreigner (3:5), a list drawn from the covenant law. The priests' failure of justice in their own teaching appears in 2:9.

sections.h: Malachi at the end of the Twelve
sections.b: Malachi is the third of the Twelve headed 'oracle' (with the two oracles of Zechariah 9-14), and it ends the Twelve with a word on the day of the LORD (4:5, as in Joel 2:31), on Edom (1:2-5, as in Obadiah), on Elijah (4:5) and on the law of Moses (4:4). The Hebrew order is Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi; the Septuagint order puts the same three last. The book closes the Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Old Testament in Protestant and most Catholic Bibles.
sections.refs: Malachi 1:1; Malachi 4:4-6; Zechariah 9:1; Zechariah 12:1; Joel 2:31; Obadiah 1:10-18

sections.b: Malachi 3:6 says 'I am the LORD, and I do not change', using shanah, a different verb from nacham, the verb of the LORD changing his mind about harm (Jonah 4:2). The two do not conflict: the first is constancy of purpose and loyalty, which explains why the sons of Jacob have not come to an end.

sections.h: The Lord comes to his temple
sections.b: Malachi 3:1 promises that the Lord the people seek will suddenly come to his temple, in answer to their question about justice. It echoes Ezekiel's vision of the glory coming into the new temple (Ezekiel 43:1-5) and the hopes of Haggai and Zechariah (Haggai 2:7-9; Zechariah 2:10-12). The irony of 3:2 is that those who seek him cannot bear his coming.

Malachi 4:2 speaks of a sun of righteousness 'with healing in its wings'. The winged sun disc is a common symbol of Egypt, Mesopotamia and Persia, and the image may use it. The Hebrew kanaf is also the wing of a bird (Psalm 17:8) or the corner of a garment (Ruth 3:9). Whether the 'wings' are rays of the sun or the LORD's sheltering wings is open.

Malachi 3:14-15 puts the old complaint of Job and Psalm 73 in the mouth of the community: the proud do well, evildoers prosper, those who test God get away with it. The book answers with the scroll of remembrance (3:16) and the day that tells the righteous from the wicked (3:18; 4:1-3).

Malachi 3:7 says 'Return to me, and I will return to you', almost the same words as Zechariah 1:3. The people reply 'How are we to return?' The answer in 3:8-10 is concrete: stop withholding the tithe and the contribution. The call belongs to the family of Jeremiah 3:12-14, Hosea 14:1-2 and Joel 2:12-13.

Malachi 1:14 puts a curse on the swindler who vows a male from his flock and then sacrifices a spoiled animal. The vow was voluntary but binding (Deuteronomy 23:21-23), and an animal with a defect was unacceptable (Leviticus 22:18-25).

The LORD promises to be a quick witness against those who wrong the widow, the fatherless and the resident foreigner, the three vulnerable groups Deuteronomy names (Deuteronomy 24:17-22). They are among the sins that Malachi 3:5 lists.

The sorcerers head the list of Malachi 3:5, as the first offense of the covenant law that Malachi names (Exodus 22:18). The Greek translates the word with a term for drug-users or poisoners (pharmakoi).

'Fear' runs through Malachi: the priests do not give the LORD the fear a master gets (1:6), Levi 'feared me' (2:5), the wicked do not fear him (3:5), and the faithful are 'those who fear the LORD' (3:16), who will see the sun of righteousness (4:2). The Plain keeps the one English 'fear'.

The LORD says 'I am a great king' and that his name is feared among the nations (1:14). The Persian ruler claimed the title 'great king', and the psalms give it to the LORD (Psalm 47:2; Psalm 95:3), so the phrase needs no Persian setting. Some hear the claim as an answer to the priests' offerings to the governor (1:8); that is a reading, not something the verse says.
Malachi 1:9 tells the priests, with irony, to 'plead with God to be kind to us', using an idiom for asking favor (Exodus 32:11; Zechariah 7:2). Their bad offerings make the plea hopeless.

The LORD says he will smear the dung of the festival sacrifices on the priests' faces and they will be carried off with it (2:3). The dung is the stomach contents of the sacrificed animals, which the law ordered burned outside the camp (Exodus 29:14; Leviticus 4:11-12).

Malachi does not use the word 'anointed' of a coming king. Two lines have been read as messianic. 3:1 promises a messenger who clears the road, then the Lord who comes to his temple, and 'the messenger of the covenant'. Jewish readers have joined this to Elijah (4:5) and the coming of the Messiah; Christians apply the messenger to John the Baptist and the Lord to Christ (Matthew 11:10). 4:2 promises a 'sun of righteousness' with healing in its wings; the Talmud reads it of a sun that heals the righteous (Avodah Zarah 3b-4a), and Christian readers from the early church have read it of Christ. The Hebrew of both lines does not name a person; the readings are receptions.
